entries.title: Your curiosity map
entries.concept: A business starts with a specific situation, not an app.
entries.build: List ten everyday frustrations and choose two you know from experience.
entries.test: Ask a family member for a recent example; if unavailable, use labeled roleplay.
entries.artifact: Map of ten problems and two hypotheses.
entries.criterion: You distinguish observation, opinion, and assumption without inventing customers.

entries.title: Observe without selling
entries.concept: Understanding the last occurrence of a problem reveals more than asking whether someone would buy.
entries.build: Prepare five neutral questions and practice listening without pitching a solution.
entries.test: Review the script with your adult and remove two leading questions.
entries.artifact: Script and notes from one authorized or simulated conversation.
entries.criterion: You can explain which question biased the response and how you changed it.

entries.title: Choose a buyer
entries.concept: The user and buyer may be different people.
entries.build: Describe three segments and who decides, uses, and pays in each.
entries.test: Find a counterexample where the person who enjoys the product cannot pay for it.
entries.criterion: The segment describes an observable situation, not everyone.

entries.title: Existing alternatives
entries.concept: A notebook or doing nothing can also be a competitor.
entries.build: Compare three current ways to solve a problem: time, cost, and limitations.
entries.test: Personally try one alternative without buying anything or creating accounts.
entries.criterion: You include doing nothing and a reason someone might prefer it.

entries.title: A small offer
entries.concept: Promise less and deliver it to learn without excessive commitments.
entries.build: Draft an offer with a buyer, task, scope, deadline, and hypothetical price.
entries.test: Ask a family member to explain the offer in their own words; correct ambiguity.
entries.criterion: Another person understands what they get and what is excluded.

entries.title: Price, cost, and time
entries.concept: A high price cannot fix an expensive or unnecessary delivery.
entries.build: Calculate three prices, delivery costs, and working hours for a fictional example.
entries.test: Simulate a refund and higher material costs; recalculate the result.
entries.criterion: You do not confuse receipts with profit and show at least one loss scenario.

entries.title: Practice an objection
entries.concept: An objection may reveal a lack of value, trust, or capacity.
entries.build: Rehearse three offer conversations with the coach in SIMULATION mode.
entries.test: Ask the coach to reject the offer for different reasons and practice accepting no.
entries.criterion: You respond without pressure and without fabricating a testimonial or guarantee.

entries.title: Deliver something small
entries.concept: Evidence of service is something another person can use.
entries.build: Prepare a free delivery for a family member: organize a file or explain a task.
entries.test: Have the family member try the result; if unavailable, document a simulated test.
entries.artifact: Before-and-after example using fictional or your own nonsensitive data.
entries.criterion: The task has a definition of done and creates no access to other people's accounts.

entries.title: Your first experiment
entries.concept: A useful test can show that your idea is wrong.
entries.build: Write the hypothesis, metric, threshold, time limit, and stopping condition before testing.
entries.test: Run an authorized or simulated test and retain an unfavorable result.
entries.criterion: The threshold existed before the result and you do not change it to claim success.

entries.title: First family defense
entries.concept: Explaining your decisions shows what you have learned.
entries.build: Prepare a three-minute demo of the problem, offer, and test.
entries.test: The adult asks three questions about evidence, cost, and what would change your mind.
entries.criterion: You distinguish learning from actual sales and propose a small next step.

entries.title: Choose the smallest complete journey
entries.concept: A minimum product lets someone complete a task, not admire features.
entries.build: Draw five user steps and reduce the journey to three.
entries.test: Try removing another step and describe when the result stops being useful.
entries.artifact: Minimum flow with inputs, outputs, and boundaries.
entries.criterion: Every step has a purpose and you can explain one feature you will not build.

entries.title: Build on paper first
entries.concept: A prototype can be a sequence of screens or a manual service.
entries.build: Make a paper or local-file prototype using synthetic data.
entries.test: Ask a family member to complete the task without explaining which button to press.
entries.criterion: You record at least one specific confusion and a correction.

entries.title: Give the AI instructions
entries.concept: A specification helps you think and verify.
entries.build: Write the objective, constraints, sample input, and expected output for one function.
entries.test: Compare the AI output with three examples, including an empty input.
entries.criterion: You recognize an AI failure and can explain the correction.

entries.title: Make a local demo
entries.concept: A working demo can exist without hosting or payments.
entries.build: Build a local screen or manual procedure for the minimum journey.
entries.test: Test normal, empty, and incorrect inputs without other people's real data.
entries.criterion: The user can finish the task and errors do not expose information.

entries.title: Minimum necessary data
entries.concept: Data you never collect does not need protection in your project.
entries.build: Inventory the data and replace real identities with synthetic information.
entries.test: Delete a fictional record and check what traces remain in your files.
entries.criterion: You explain the purpose of every data item and remove one unnecessary item.

entries.title: Test the experience
entries.concept: The builder understanding a screen does not prove someone else can use it.
entries.build: Define a task and observe a family test or roleplay.
entries.test: Record where the test stalled and change just one thing.
entries.criterion: You distinguish comments from behavior and do not generalize from one person.

entries.title: Explain without exaggeration
entries.concept: A clear page describes what already works.
entries.build: Write a headline, example, scope, and invitation to a private test.
entries.test: Underline outcome claims and remove any unsupported by evidence.
entries.criterion: You do not call an outcome guaranteed when it depends on the customer.

entries.title: Delivery and support
entries.concept: Selling includes responding when something goes wrong.
entries.build: Design usage instructions, adult-managed contact, and a correction policy.
entries.test: Simulate a complaint, an error, and an out-of-scope request.
entries.artifact: Delivery guide and three support responses.
entries.criterion: Each case has an owner and a remedy you can honor.

entries.title: Tool limits
entries.concept: More agents can increase cost and confusion.
entries.build: Compare doing a task manually, with one coach, and with two successive roles.
entries.test: Measure time and quality on the same fictional task without creating permanent bots.
entries.criterion: You choose the sufficient approach and explain what does not run at rest.

entries.title: Product demo
entries.concept: A demo should show the journey and its limitations.
entries.build: Present the original task, current version, and two known failures.
entries.test: Your adult or teammate repeats a test and identifies something still unclear.
entries.criterion: You disclose limitations and do not present a simulation as real traction.

entries.title: Choose a demand test
entries.concept: Clicks, compliments, and money are different signals.
entries.build: Define what behavior would indicate interest and what would not prove it.
entries.test: Build an evidence ladder: opinion, attempt, commitment, and actual payment.
entries.criterion: You can describe a false positive in your test.

entries.title: Distribute with permission
entries.concept: A small relevant channel can teach more than mass publication.
entries.build: Prepare a draft for two approved contacts or a fictional audience.
entries.test: Compare two messages through roleplay and get adult review before sending either.
entries.criterion: You do not send automatically or persist after rejection.

entries.title: Decide with limited data
entries.concept: A small sample guides questions; it does not establish a law.
entries.build: Organize results, including zeros and rejections, in a table.
entries.test: Ask the coach for an alternative explanation and design a way to distinguish it.
entries.criterion: You identify selection bias and do not claim statistical significance without support.

entries.title: Review unit economics
entries.concept: Every sale should contribute toward other costs.
entries.build: Calculate receipts net of refunds, direct cost, and contribution per delivery.
entries.test: Simulate double the working time and one refund among five sales.
entries.criterion: You do not call contribution margin net margin.

entries.title: Learn from retention
entries.concept: Repeat usage may indicate value, but not every purchase should recur.
entries.build: Map how a user gets value and why they would or would not return.
entries.test: Interview a family member about a product they stopped using, or use roleplay.
entries.artifact: Usage map and two abandonment hypotheses.
entries.criterion: You do not add a subscription to a need that does not recur.

entries.title: Change one variable
entries.concept: Changing everything at once hides what caused the difference.
entries.build: Choose one variable: message, scope, or price; write what stays fixed.
entries.test: Test two simulated variants or use an authorized group and preserve the limitations.
entries.criterion: You do not present an informal test as a conclusive causal experiment.

entries.title: Close a learning cycle
entries.concept: Closing an idea preserves time and learning.
entries.build: Review three tests and choose to continue, narrow, pivot, or close.
entries.test: Write the strongest argument against your decision and respond with evidence.
entries.criterion: The decision includes the cost of continuing and a future condition for reconsideration.

entries.title: Content that helps
entries.concept: You can teach what you learned without public exposure.
entries.build: Write a short guide to a problem in your field using your own example.
entries.test: Have a family member follow it; record where they need help.
entries.criterion: You use your own words, credit references, and do not copy a book or video.

entries.title: Test again
entries.concept: A useful iteration responds to a specific observation.
entries.build: Implement one improvement based on a documented failure.
entries.test: Repeat the same task and compare time, errors, and limits of the comparison.
entries.criterion: The improvement responds to evidence rather than aesthetic preference alone.

entries.title: Demand review
entries.concept: Being honest about missing demand enables a good decision.
entries.build: Present metrics, rejections, costs, and lessons from the quarter.
entries.test: Defend why you would run another test or close the project.
entries.criterion: You can pass without revenue when the reasoning and evidence are strong.

entries.title: Document a delivery
entries.concept: An understandable process reduces errors without automating everything.
entries.build: Write an SOP for a task you have already repeated.
entries.test: Have a family member or teammate follow it with fictional data without your help.
entries.criterion: It includes inputs, steps, quality, owner, and error handling.

entries.title: Automate once
entries.concept: Automate a task you understand, with limits and a measurable return.
entries.build: Prepare a local script or reusable instruction for one small task.
entries.test: Run it once with normal, empty, and failure cases; add no recurrence.
entries.criterion: You can stop it and demonstrate that no scheduled tasks exist.

entries.title: Negotiate scope
entries.concept: Agreeing on boundaries protects both sides.
entries.build: Rehearse two scope options with different fictional deadlines and prices.
entries.test: A customer role asks for an extra; practice explaining what changes in the agreement.
entries.artifact: Simulated agreement with scope and limits.
entries.criterion: You do not promise outcomes beyond your control to close the conversation.

entries.title: Cash and commitments
entries.concept: Having money in an account does not mean you can spend it all.
entries.build: Make a fictional calendar of receipts, payments, and refund reserves.
entries.test: Delay a receipt by one week and check whether you can still fund delivery.
entries.criterion: You distinguish financing, available cash, and provisional profit.

entries.title: Rights and publication
entries.concept: Being able to view material does not grant redistribution rights.
entries.build: Inventory images, text, code, and data in your demo with their provenance.
entries.test: Replace a resource of uncertain rights with your own or an authorized one.
entries.criterion: You include no private content or implied endorsement merely because you cite someone.

entries.title: Working as a team
entries.concept: Collaboration requires clear contributions and ways to resolve disagreement.
entries.build: Define roles, deliverables, hours, and what happens if someone leaves.
entries.test: Rehearse a disagreement over quality or workload with an adult moderator.
entries.criterion: Everyone can explain their contribution and there is a respectful exit path.

entries.title: Audit your numbers
entries.concept: A trustworthy record includes errors and visible corrections.
entries.build: Check duplicates, currency, mode, and references in your ledger.
entries.test: Insert a duplicate into a copy and confirm the tool rejects it.
entries.artifact: Clean ledger and list of missing costs.
entries.criterion: You never count investment or simulations as real profit.

entries.title: Assess AI risks
entries.concept: A convincing answer can be incorrect or contain inappropriate data.
entries.build: List three ways your coach or product could fail.
entries.test: Test one fictional case for each risk and define review or reduced scope.
entries.criterion: You distinguish model instructions from real technical controls.

entries.title: Defend the portfolio
entries.concept: A defense checks understanding, not just appearance.
entries.build: Choose five pieces of evidence and rehearse the fifteen-minute presentation.
entries.test: An adult or mentor questions the main figure, AI contribution, and weakest decision.
entries.artifact: Portfolio and defense with recorded questions.
entries.criterion: You explain evidence, uncertainty, and mistakes without inventing results.

entries.title: Choose your next year
entries.concept: Continuing, changing, and closing are all founder decisions.
entries.build: Design a ten-week plan with a hypothesis, workload, and budget.
entries.test: Compare it with closing the project and starting something smaller.
entries.criterion: The plan respects school and rest and does not depend on reaching a million.
